 Appendix B - Hyperledger Fabric Architecture Alignment 17
 1.0 Blockchain Platform Technical Proposal
 The proposed REC Portal will use Hyperledger Fabric as a permissioned trust layer behind the portal. Business users will continue to work through normal portal screens and APIs. Fabric will record and validate selected REC lifecycle events where shared trust, traceability and multi-organisation control are important.
 The design keeps sensitive information outside the blockchain. Personal details, uploaded documents, payment information and operational records remain in secured enterprise systems. The ledger stores only the REC state, approved references, transaction history and cryptographic proof required for audit and verification.
 Design principle Use blockchain where it adds shared trust. Keep user experience, documents, reporting and normal business processing in the portal and enterprise data layer.
 1.0.1 Requirement Alignment
 RFP Area
 High-Level Response
 9.1 Platform Selection
 Hyperledger Fabric 2.5.x permissioned network with chaincode, identity, privacy and consortium controls.
 9.2 Distributed Node Architecture
 Stakeholder-aligned Fabric organisations and peers, with controlled access and resilient cloud deployment.
 9.3 Smart Contract Support
 Fabric chaincode for selected REC lifecycle rules, governed through the Fabric chaincode lifecycle.
 9.4 Privacy & Security
 Sensitive data kept off-chain; Fabric identities, TLS, endorsement policies and private data used where appropriate.
 9.5 Consortium Management
 Governed membership, organisation policies, chaincode approval and network configuration changes.
 9.6 Identity Integration
 Portal identity linked with organisation and Fabric X.509 identity through MSP-based trust.
 9.7-9.12 Other Requirements
 DSC, API security, DR/BCP, performance, SLA and license management addressed at a high level without unnecessary bid-stage commitments.
 1.1 Platform Selection
 1.1.1 Name and Version
 Hyperledger Fabric 2.5.x LTS is proposed as the blockchain platform. Fabric is designed for permissioned enterprise networks where participating organisations are known and where access, transaction approval and data visibility must be controlled. This matches the REC Portal, which is a regulated registry rather than an open public blockchain.
 1.1.2 Rationale for Selection
 Hyperledger Fabric is selected because its core architecture maps naturally to the REC operating model. It separates identity, transaction endorsement, ordering and ledger commit, allowing the network to apply business controls without giving a single technical component complete authority over a transaction.
 Selection Area
 Why it is suitable for the REC Portal
 Permissioned participation
 Fabric uses organisations, Membership Service Providers (MSPs) and X.509 certificates so only approved members and services can interact with the network.
 Multi-organisation control
 Endorsement policies can require approval from the relevant organisations before an REC state change is accepted. This supports shared governance and reduces unilateral action.
 Smart contracts
 Chaincode can enforce selected REC lifecycle rules such as eligibility checks, issuance, ownership change, blocking, redemption and status controls in a consistent way.
 Privacy
 Sensitive information can remain off-chain. Private Data Collections can be used where selected consortium members need to share restricted business data while other members only retain proof of the transaction.
 Auditability
 Committed transactions carry an ordered, tamper-evident history linked to authenticated identities, giving a clear technical trail for REC lifecycle events.
 Enterprise integration
 Fabric Gateway and SDK/API patterns allow the portal and connected systems to use blockchain without exposing peer-level complexity to end users.
 No cryptocurrency dependency
 Fabric does not require mining, a native cryptocurrency or gas fees. This is appropriate for a regulated certificate registry.
 Controlled evolution
 Membership, policies and chaincode can be updated through governed Fabric configuration and lifecycle processes without replacing the full platform.
 RFP alignment This directly addresses the requirement for smart contracts, privacy, consortium management, security, scalability and performance suitability while keeping the design technology-focused and implementation-neutral.
 1.2 Distributed Node Architecture
 The network will follow a stakeholder-aligned Hyperledger Fabric organisation model. NLDC and RLDC responsibilities are represented through separate logical organisation boundaries, identities and permissions. The exact infrastructure quantities, server sizes and cloud resource values are not fixed in this proposal and will be confirmed during detailed design.
 Fabric Layer
 Role in the REC architecture
 Organisation / MSP
 Defines the trusted boundary for a stakeholder organisation, its identities and the policies under which it participates.
 Peer
 Maintains the ledger and world state, runs or connects to chaincode, validates transactions and may endorse transactions according to policy.
 Ordering service
 Establishes a common transaction order and creates blocks. It does not replace endorsement or business-rule validation.
 Channel
 Provides the shared ledger context for authorised consortium organisations. Channel design will be kept as simple as possible to avoid unnecessary fragmentation.
 Private Data Collection
 Allows selected organisations to share restricted business data while the channel retains cryptographic evidence of the transaction.
 Fabric Gateway
 Provides the application-facing path for transaction submission, query, endorsement handling and commit confirmation.
 Off-chain enterprise services
 Hold PII, documents, payments, searchable reporting data and other information that does not need to be replicated on blockchain.
 1.2.1 Stakeholder Node Deployment
 Fabric peers will be associated with the required stakeholder organisations and hosted on MeitY-empanelled cloud/data-centre infrastructure in line with the RFP. Production and backup deployment will use separate seismic zones. Detailed peer placement, ordering-service topology, compute, storage and scaling values will be finalised after workload and availability validation.
 The logical organisation boundary is more important than the physical server location: each stakeholder organisation retains a distinct Fabric identity and policy boundary even when the underlying infrastructure is cloud-hosted.
 1.2.2 Node Access and Permissions
 Normal portal users will not connect directly to Fabric peers. They will use the REC Portal and secured application services.
 Fabric MSPs and X.509 certificates will identify organisations, services and blockchain clients.
 Roles and identity attributes can be checked by application services and chaincode before a state-changing function is allowed.
 Peer administration, chaincode lifecycle actions and network configuration will use separate privileged identities and controlled change processes.
 Read, submit, endorse and administer permissions will be treated separately rather than giving broad access to one role.
 1.2.3 Network Security and Integrity
 TLS/mTLS will protect communication between authorised services and Fabric components.
 Fabric certificate-based identity and revocation mechanisms will control network membership.
 Endorsement policies will define which organisation approvals are required for important transactions.
 The ordering service will provide deterministic transaction ordering, while peers will still validate endorsements and transaction rules before state is updated.
 Ledger hashes, transaction history and monitoring will support integrity checks and investigation of abnormal behaviour.
 1.2.4 Data Privacy and Compliance
 The data-placement rule is simple: blockchain stores trusted state and proof; enterprise systems store detailed content. Personal data, identity documents, uploaded evidence, credentials, bank/payment information and free-form records remain off-chain. The ledger stores REC identifiers, quantities, lifecycle status, approvals, references and hashes where integrity proof is useful.
 Private Data Collections may be used for limited inter-organisation data sharing when there is a clear need for selected Fabric members to see the actual payload. Channels will not be created only for data privacy if a simpler private-data or off-chain approach is sufficient.
 1.2.5 Scalability and Interoperability
 The architecture separates the portal, API, query/reporting, event-processing and blockchain layers so each can scale independently. New organisations can be admitted through Fabric membership and configuration changes. External systems such as exchanges, identity services and other registries can integrate through versioned APIs and events rather than direct access to peers.
 No fixed sizing commitment Infrastructure counts, transaction throughput and latency values will be confirmed during detailed design and testing against the agreed REC workload.
 1.3 Smart Contract Support Requirements
 Hyperledger Fabric chaincode will automate only the REC rules that benefit from common, tamper-evident enforcement across organisations. Document checking, manual regulatory judgment and other processes that require external evidence can remain off-chain, with the approved outcome referenced on the ledger.
 1.3.1 Programming Language
 Go is proposed as the primary chaincode language because it is well supported in Hyperledger Fabric, has a simple deployment model and is suitable for deterministic business logic. Other Fabric-supported languages can be considered where there is a clear project need, but a single primary language keeps maintenance simpler.
 1.3.2 Development and Testing
 Area
 High-Level Approach
 Business logic
 Model REC operations as clear state transitions with validation before each change.
 Authorisation
 Check the caller organisation, role and required endorsements rather than trusting values supplied in the request body.
 Data handling
 Keep sensitive or large documents outside chaincode; store only required references, state and hashes.
 Testing
 Use unit and integration testing for normal, invalid and authorisation scenarios before deployment.
 Integration
 Expose chaincode through the blockchain gateway and application APIs, not directly to portal users.
 1.3.3 Lifecycle and Upgrades
 Fabric chaincode lifecycle will be used to package, approve and commit smart-contract versions. An upgrade changes the approved chaincode definition while preserving the existing ledger. This supports regulatory rule changes without replacing the blockchain or moving the full history to a new system.
 Changes will be versioned and reviewed before production use.
 Relevant consortium organisations will approve chaincode definitions according to the agreed governance model.
 Where possible, business parameters will be separated from code so routine approved changes do not require unnecessary redevelopment.
 Any data-model change that affects existing ledger state will be designed and reconciled separately rather than hidden inside a normal upgrade.
 1.3.4 Deployment and Maintenance
 Chaincode deployment will follow the project release process with source control, testing and authorised approval. Maintenance will focus on regulatory changes, security fixes and compatibility with the agreed Fabric release. Detailed tools, pipeline products and release-frequency commitments will be finalised with GRID-INDIA during implementation.
 RFP alignment The approach covers programming language, tools/frameworks, lifecycle management, upgradability, deployment and maintenance while avoiding unnecessary tool-specific commitments at bid stage.
 1.4 Privacy and Security Features
 1.4.1 Privacy Mechanisms
 Privacy is achieved by combining Fabric controls with normal enterprise data protection. Not every data item needs to be placed on a distributed ledger. The design therefore keeps sensitive content off-chain and uses blockchain mainly for shared state, approvals and proof.
 Data / Control
 Recommended Treatment
 REC lifecycle facts
 Store on-chain where they are required for shared verification and state control.
 Ownership reference
 Store a controlled or pseudonymous reference on-chain; keep personally identifiable mapping off-chain.
 Approvals and transaction history
 Record on-chain so the sequence of approved changes is traceable.
 Personal information
 Keep in secured off-chain systems with role-based access.
 Documents and evidence
 Keep off-chain; store a hash/reference on-chain where integrity proof is useful.
 Restricted inter-organisation data
 Use Fabric Private Data Collections or a restricted off-chain exchange depending on the business need.
 Payment / bank information
 Keep outside the blockchain in the appropriate payment or finance environment.
 1.4.2 Security Controls
 Fabric / Security Control
 Purpose
 MSP and X.509 certificates
 Establish trusted organisation and client identity.
 TLS / mTLS
 Protect service-to-service and Fabric network communication.
 Endorsement policies
 Require the agreed organisation approvals before selected transactions can update state.
 Access control and attributes
 Restrict chaincode functions and administrative actions to authorised roles.
 Private Data Collections
 Limit selected business data to authorised Fabric members while retaining ledger evidence.
 Ledger immutability and hashes
 Provide a tamper-evident history for committed transactions and referenced evidence.
 Key and certificate management
 Protect blockchain identities and support certificate renewal/revocation under controlled procedures.
 Monitoring and audit logs
 Support operational monitoring, security review and investigation without placing sensitive payloads in logs.
 Security controls will be aligned with the project security architecture and applicable GRID-INDIA requirements. Detailed encryption settings, key-storage products, retention periods and security-tool choices will be confirmed during detailed design.
 1.5 Consortium Management
 The REC blockchain will operate as a permissioned consortium. In Hyperledger Fabric, consortium governance is expressed through organisation membership, MSP definitions, channel policies, endorsement policies and the chaincode lifecycle. This allows participation and technical authority to follow the real REC governance structure.
 1.5.1 Participant Management
 Lifecycle Step
 High-Level Fabric Approach
 Onboard organisation
 Verify the organisation, establish its MSP/certificate trust, define approved roles and add it through governed network configuration.
 Onboard service/user
 Issue or map the required identity, assign role attributes and grant only the needed portal/blockchain permissions.
 Change role or access
 Update off-chain role mapping and, where required, certificate attributes or Fabric policy/configuration.
 Revoke access
 Revoke or expire the relevant credentials so future transactions are blocked while historical ledger records remain unchanged.
 Add or replace infrastructure
 Change peer/service endpoints within the organisation boundary without changing historical ownership or transaction records.
 1.5.2 Governance Model
 Governance Area
 High-Level Approach
 Membership changes
 Require an approved consortium change before adding/removing an organisation from the Fabric configuration.
 Endorsement policy
 Define which organisations must approve important REC state changes. Exact combinations will be agreed with GRID-INDIA.
 Chaincode changes
 Use the Fabric lifecycle so required organisations approve a chaincode definition before it is committed.
 Channel / policy changes
 Use authorised configuration updates with an auditable record of the resulting network configuration.
 Private data changes
 Review member visibility before changing a collection because privacy membership directly affects who can receive data.
 Operational decisions
 Keep normal infrastructure operations separate from business approvals; operating a peer does not automatically grant authority to change REC state.
 The ordering service provides transaction ordering and availability support, but it is not treated as the business approval authority. Business authority comes from authenticated clients, chaincode rules and endorsement policies. This separation is an important reason Fabric fits a multi-stakeholder REC registry.
 Governance principle No single technical administrator should gain business authority merely because they operate infrastructure. Fabric separates infrastructure roles from endorsement and application permissions.
 1.6 Identity Integration Requirements
 Identity will be implemented in layers so user login, legal signing and blockchain permission remain distinct. This keeps the user experience simple while allowing Fabric to enforce organisation-level trust.
 1.6.1 Identity Management Framework
 Identity Layer
 Role in the Solution
 Portal identity
 Authenticates the user and controls screens, workflows and application roles.
 Organisation identity
 Links the user or service to an approved REC stakeholder organisation.
 Fabric X.509 identity
 Allows an authorised blockchain client/service to submit, query or endorse transactions under an MSP.
 Identity attributes
 Carry or map role/organisation information used by services and chaincode for authorisation.
 DSC identity
 Provides user-level signing evidence for transactions where the business process requires a Digital Signature Certificate.
 Personal identity information will remain in the portal or approved identity system. The blockchain should use only the minimum identity reference needed for authorisation and audit.
 1.6.2 Verification and Authentication
 User signs in through the approved portal identity mechanism.
 The application confirms the user role, organisation and permission for the requested action.
 Where required, the user signs the business payload through the approved DSC process.
 The blockchain gateway submits the authorised request using the appropriate Fabric client identity.
 Chaincode and Fabric policies validate caller identity, business rules and required endorsements before state is committed.
 The final transaction reference is linked back to the portal audit trail for authorised review.
 1.6.3 Interoperability and Compatibility
 The identity layer will use standards-based integration so existing enterprise or government identity systems can be connected without putting provider-specific logic inside chaincode. Fabric will rely on trusted certificate/MSP identity and approved attributes, while adapters or application services translate external identity information into the form required by the portal and blockchain gateway.
 This approach allows identity providers, login mechanisms or connected registries to evolve without changing the REC ledger model. Detailed identity-provider products and authentication standards will be selected based on GRID-INDIA integration requirements.
 RFP alignment The design addresses identity framework, verification/authentication and interoperability while keeping PII off-chain and using Fabric MSP/X.509 identity for blockchain trust.
 1.7 Digital Signature Certificates (DSCs)
 Where a transaction requires DSC approval, the portal will present the business information for signing. The approved signing mechanism will return the signature or validation result without exposing the user private key to the blockchain application. After verification, the blockchain gateway submits the corresponding Fabric transaction.
 Step
 High-Level Flow
 Review
 User reviews the transaction and approval details in the portal.
 Sign
 User signs using the approved DSC method where required.
 Verify
 Application verifies the signature, certificate status and signer mapping.
 Authorise
 Portal/Fabric permissions and business prerequisites are checked.
 Submit
 Blockchain gateway sends the transaction for Fabric endorsement and commit.
 Confirm
 Portal shows the final status and blockchain transaction reference.
 1.8 API Management and Security
 An API management layer will protect portal and external interfaces. A separate blockchain gateway service will handle Fabric Gateway/SDK interaction so Fabric-specific details remain isolated from the main REC application.
 Authenticate and authorise API clients and users.
 Use encrypted channels for trusted system integrations.
 Apply reasonable rate controls and request validation.
 Use correlation identifiers and central logging for traceability.
 Expose stable versioned interfaces to exchanges and other connected systems.
 1.9 Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity
 The distributed ledger provides replicated committed history across authorised Fabric peers. If a peer or its world-state database is unavailable, it can be restored or resynchronised from trusted blockchain data. Off-chain databases and document stores will use standard enterprise backup, replication and restore procedures.
 Area
 High-Level Recovery Approach
 Fabric ledger
 Recover or resynchronise from trusted peers or verified snapshots/backup as supported by the final design.
 World state
 Rebuild from the ledger where required.
 Application database
 Use encrypted backup/replication and documented restore procedures.
 Document store
 Use protected backup and integrity checks.
 Keys and certificates
 Use controlled recovery, re-issuance and revocation procedures as applicable.
 Recovery objectives, drill frequency, failover design and detailed operational procedures will be agreed with GRID-INDIA and DRDTC during implementation rather than committed as fixed values in this high-level proposal.
 1.10 Performance and Scalability
 The design keeps routine searches, dashboards and reports away from direct blockchain dependency. Read-heavy functions can use application projections and caches updated from Fabric events, while Fabric remains the trusted source for important REC state changes.
 Scale portal, API and reporting services independently from Fabric peers.
 Use indexed and bounded ledger queries and avoid large unbounded scans inside chaincode.
 Use event-driven application projections for search and reporting.
 Tune block, endorsement and gateway settings after representative workload testing.
 Confirm throughput, latency and infrastructure sizing during detailed design and pre-production testing.
 No additional benchmark commitment The proposal does not introduce fixed performance numbers beyond the RFP/contract. Final acceptance values will follow the agreed requirements and tested workload.
 1.11 Service Level Agreement (SLA) Framework
 The final SLA will follow the tender and contract. It will cover service availability, support response, transaction processing, monitoring, reporting and escalation. Exact targets will be aligned with Clause 12.0 and the final production design rather than adding separate bid-stage commitments.
 1.12 Software License Management
 The project will maintain a simple record of the main software, platforms, libraries and third-party products used in the REC Portal. Relevant open-source and commercial license conditions will be reviewed and the necessary license information will be included in project documentation.
 Vara will collaborate with RESL on the blockchain workstream for the REC Portal. The objective is to design and develop a secure, scalable and permissioned Hyperledger Fabric based blockchain layer that can integrate cleanly with the wider REC Portal. The detailed division of responsibilities will be finalised jointly wherever the blockchain work depends on portal, infrastructure, identity or external-system inputs.
 2.0 Scope of Work
 2.1 Key Work Areas
 2.1.1 Blockchain Platform Selection
 Validate Hyperledger Fabric as the blockchain platform for the REC use case and confirm the appropriate supported version during detailed design.
 Define the logical stakeholder organisation and node model and the required communication paths between blockchain participants.
 2.1.2 Blockchain Technical Architecture
 Define the main Hyperledger Fabric components, including organisations/MSPs, peers, ordering service, Certificate Authorities, channels or Private Data Collections, chaincode and gateway integration.
 Jointly define the on-chain and off-chain data boundary so the blockchain design remains aligned with the web application, privacy requirements and business workflows.
 Keep infrastructure sizing and final hosting ownership outside this scope until RESL and Vara agree the environment and deployment responsibility.
 2.1.3 Smart Contract and Chaincode Development
 Design and develop chaincode for agreed REC lifecycle functions such as issuance, digital representation/tokenisation, transfer/trading controls, redemption and related state changes.
 Confirm the chaincode language, development tools and supporting frameworks for the project.
 Use the Hyperledger Fabric chaincode lifecycle so contract versions and upgrades can be managed through controlled consortium approval.
 2.1.4 Privacy and Security Implementation
 Apply Fabric-native security controls such as MSP-based identity, X.509 certificates, TLS/mTLS, endorsement policies and controlled peer access.
 Use channels, Private Data Collections, hashes and off-chain storage where appropriate to limit the exposure of sensitive data.
 Coordinate with the wider application security design because privacy and authentication span both the blockchain and web-application layers.
 2.1.5 Consortium Management
 Define participant onboarding, node setup, organisation identity, permissions and governance processes for the Fabric consortium.
 Vara will develop and validate the blockchain configuration in the development environment and support RESL during test and production deployment. Final infrastructure ownership and operational responsibilities will be agreed jointly.
 2.1.6 Identity Integration and Digital Signatures
 Jointly review the existing identity provider and Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) model before finalising the blockchain identity design.
 Integrate portal authentication, DSC-based business signing where required, and Fabric X.509 identities without placing personal identity data directly on-chain.
 Confirm how user certificates, dongles or other signing mechanisms interact with the portal and blockchain transaction flow.
 2.1.7 API and Data Management
 Provide REST APIs or a blockchain gateway microservice for controlled interaction between the REC Portal and the Hyperledger Fabric network.
 Maintain required off-chain transaction/request metadata and blockchain read models for application queries, reporting and operational traceability. The blockchain ledger remains the authoritative source for committed on-chain state.
 2.1.8 Historical Data Migration
 Vara and RESL will jointly decide which historical REC data should be represented on-chain and which data should remain off-chain.
 Vara will prepare blockchain migration scripts based on the agreed migration approach, while execution and reconciliation will be carried out collaboratively where upstream or downstream scripts are interdependent.
 2.2 Work Breakdown and Responsibilities
 The following work breakdown captures the current understanding of responsibilities. Items marked as joint or dependent will be finalised during design discussions between Vara and RESL.
 2.2.1 Platform Selection

 Task
 Responsible Team
 Notes / Dependency
 Identity integration framework
 Vara with RESL inputs
 Define how authenticated portal identities map to Fabric identities and blockchain permissions.
 Interoperability and compatibility
 Both
 Review the existing identity provider and agree the integration approach before fixing detailed responsibilities.
 Digital Signature Certificates (DSC)
 Both
 Agree how DSC signing, user-side certificates/dongles and blockchain transaction submission will interact.
 2.2.7 API and Data Management
 Task
 Responsible Team
 Notes / Dependency
 Blockchain gateway / REST APIs
 Vara
 Develop the service interface used by the REC Portal to submit blockchain transactions and queries.
 Off-chain blockchain transaction data
 Vara
 Maintain the agreed off-chain request, transaction and block metadata/read models needed for portal queries, reporting and operational traceability.
 2.2.8 Historical Data Migration
 Task
 Responsible Team
 Notes / Dependency
 Migration strategy
 Both
 Agree the historical data boundary and decide what must be represented on-chain.
 Blockchain migration scripts
 Vara
 Prepare scripts for blockchain migration according to the jointly agreed strategy.
 Migration execution and reconciliation
 Both
 Coordinate execution where blockchain and application migration activities depend on each other.
 2.3 Key Dependencies and Discussion Points
 The existing identity-management framework and DSC distribution model need to be reviewed jointly. In particular, the teams should confirm how certificate dongles or other signing methods will be used before transactions are submitted to Hyperledger Fabric.
 Multiple signatories may add operational complexity. The required signing and endorsement model should therefore be agreed from actual REC approval workflows rather than assumed at design stage.
 Changes to channel/private-data policies, identity roles or chaincode access rules can require configuration and code changes. Governance for such changes should be kept controlled and as simple as the RFP permits.
 Infrastructure ownership, cloud provisioning, access to development/test/production environments and operating responsibility need to be agreed separately between Vara and RESL.
 The on-chain/off-chain data boundary is a joint design decision because the REC Portal includes both blockchain and conventional web-application components.
 2.4 Scope Conclusion
 This Scope of Work defines the main blockchain responsibilities for Vara and the areas that require joint decisions with RESL. The focus is on a practical Hyperledger Fabric implementation with clear permissioning, controlled smart contracts, secure integration and a well-defined data boundary. Detailed infrastructure sizing, final hosting ownership, identity-provider integration and migration execution will be confirmed collaboratively during detailed design.
 Appendix A - Technical Assumptions and Clarifications
 The final Hyperledger Fabric patch release and supporting cloud services will be confirmed during detailed design.
 Infrastructure quantities, server sizing and detailed topology values are intentionally excluded from this high-level proposal.
 Final endorsement policies, channel/private-data design, identity mappings and chaincode rules will be agreed with GRID-INDIA.
 Performance targets and SLA values will follow the tender/contract and will be validated during testing.
 External integration details depend on final interface specifications and test credentials for the connected systems.
 Appendix B - Hyperledger Fabric Architecture Alignment
 Fabric Concept
 Use in the REC Portal
 Organisation / MSP
 Represents trusted consortium organisations and their blockchain membership.
 Certificate Authority / X.509
 Supports trusted identity issuance and certificate-based authentication.
 Peer
 Maintains ledger/state and validates or endorses transactions as allowed by policy.
 Ordering service
 Creates a common transaction order and distributes blocks; it does not replace business endorsement.
 Chaincode
 Implements selected REC business rules and state transitions.
 Channel
 Provides a shared ledger context for authorised consortium members.
 Private Data Collection
 Supports restricted data sharing among selected members without creating unnecessary channels.
 Endorsement policy
 Defines which organisations must approve selected transactions before state can change.
 Fabric Gateway
 Provides the application-facing transaction/query path and hides peer-level details from the portal.
 Ledger + world state
 Ledger keeps immutable transaction history; world state provides the current queryable state.
 Summary The proposed design uses Hyperledger Fabric as a permissioned trust layer behind the REC Portal. It aligns with the RFP while remaining high-level, avoids unnecessary infrastructure and performance commitments, and keeps sensitive business content outside the ledger unless restricted Fabric sharing is clearly required.

 SALE AGREEMENT
 This Sale Agreement (the "Agreement") is made and executed on 30 September 2026 (the "Agreement Date") by and between the following parties:
 1. Apex Industrial Assets Private Limited, a company incorporated under the laws of India, having its registered office at 201, Western Business Centre, Andheri East, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400069, hereinafter referred to as the "Seller"; and
 2. LMN Asset Pvt. Ltd., a company incorporated under the laws of India, having its registered office at 501, Business Tower, Andheri East, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400069, hereinafter referred to as the "Purchaser".
 The Seller and the Purchaser are individually referred to as a "Party" and collectively as the "Parties".
 RECITALS
 A. The Seller represents that it is the lawful owner of the commercial office premises described in Schedule 1 (the "Property") and has the right and authority to sell and transfer the Property.
 B. The Purchaser has agreed to purchase the Property from the Seller for the consideration and on the terms set out in this Agreement.
 C. The Parties wish to record the terms governing the sale, purchase, transfer of title, payment, possession, registration and completion of the transaction.
 1. DEFINITIONS
 Term
 Meaning
 Agreement
 This Sale Agreement together with its Schedules and any written amendments.
 Completion
 The completion of the sale and purchase upon satisfaction of the applicable conditions and delivery of the Completion Documents.
 Completion Date
 30 September 2026, or another date agreed in writing by the Parties.
 Encumbrance

 Purchase Price

 Property
 The commercial office premises described in Schedule 1, together with the rights and appurtenances expressly included in the sale.
 Completion Documents
 The title, transfer, possession, tax, statutory and other documents specified in Schedule 3.
 2. AGREEMENT TO SELL AND PURCHASE
 2.1 The Seller agrees to sell, convey, assign and transfer the Property to the Purchaser, and the Purchaser agrees to purchase and accept the Property, free from all undisclosed Encumbrances and third-party claims.
 2.2 The sale includes the Property and all rights, easements, access rights, common-area rights and appurtenant rights legally attached to it, together with the fixtures and improvements expressly included in Schedule 1.
 2.3 The Seller shall not sell, agree to sell, mortgage, lease, license, encumber or otherwise dispose of the Property between the Agreement Date and Completion.
 3. PURCHASE PRICE
 3.1 The total Purchase Price for the Property is ₹12,50,00,000 (Rupees Twelve Crore Fifty Lakh Only).
 3.2 The Parties acknowledge that the Purchase Price is consistent with the indicative valuation conclusion of ₹12.50 crore contained in the related valuation memorandum dated 30 September 2026.
 3.3 The Purchase Price is subject to applicable taxes, duties and statutory charges as allocated under Clause 9 and Schedule 2.
 4. PAYMENT TERMS
 4.1 The Purchaser shall pay the Purchase Price as follows:
 a) ₹1,25,00,000 as earnest money/deposit, payable on execution of this Agreement;
 b) ₹3,75,00,000 as the second instalment upon satisfaction of the conditions precedent and completion of agreed title due diligence; and
 c) ₹7,50,00,000 as the balance consideration at Completion against delivery of the Completion Documents, possession and execution/registration of the applicable transfer instrument.
 4.2 Payments shall be made through normal banking channels to the Seller's designated account, subject to applicable law.
 4.3 The Seller shall issue appropriate receipts and tax invoices/documents where legally required.
 5. CONDITIONS PRECEDENT
 Completion is conditional upon: (a) satisfactory verification of the Seller's title; (b) confirmation that the Property is free of undisclosed Encumbrances; (c) verification of applicable approvals and permitted commercial use; (d) receipt of required corporate, regulatory or third-party approvals; (e) no material adverse litigation or governmental action affecting the Property; and (f) execution of all required ancillary documents.
 6. TITLE AND SELLER'S COVENANTS
 6.1 The Seller represents and warrants that it has good, valid and transferable title to the Property and full authority to enter into and complete the sale.
 6.2 The Seller shall provide the Purchaser with copies/originals, as applicable, of title deeds, prior conveyances, sanctioned plans, completion/occupancy documentation, tax records, society/association records and other relevant property documents.
 6.3 The Seller shall discharge all monetary liabilities, taxes, maintenance dues, utility dues and other obligations attributable to the period up to Completion, unless expressly allocated otherwise in Schedule 2.
 6.4 The Seller shall procure release/discharge of any disclosed mortgage or other Encumbrance before or simultaneously with Completion.
 7. INSPECTION AND PROPERTY CONDITION
 7.1 The Purchaser shall have reasonable access to inspect the Property and its documents before Completion.
 7.2 The Property shall be delivered in substantially the condition represented by the Seller, subject to ordinary wear and tear.
 7.3 Inspection or acceptance shall not waive the Purchaser's rights in respect of fraud, defective title, concealed defects or breach of the Seller's express representations and warranties.
 8. COMPLETION, POSSESSION AND TRANSFER
 8.1 Completion shall occur on 30 September 2026 at [registered office/sub-registrar office/other agreed location], subject to satisfaction of the conditions precedent.
 8.2 At Completion, the Seller shall deliver vacant and peaceful possession of the Property to the Purchaser, unless Schedule 1 expressly states otherwise.
 8.3 The Parties shall execute and register the applicable sale deed/conveyance or other instrument required to transfer legal title.
 8.4 Risk in the Property shall pass to the Purchaser upon Completion and delivery of possession, except to the extent caused by the Seller's breach or wilful misconduct.
 8.5 The Seller shall cooperate with mutation, registration, society/association transfer and other post-completion formalities.
 9. TAXES, STAMP DUTY AND REGISTRATION
 9.1 Stamp duty and registration charges relating to the instrument of transfer shall be borne by the Purchaser unless mandatory law requires otherwise.
 9.2 Taxes attributable to the Seller's ownership or period before Completion shall be borne by the Seller.
 9.3 Any applicable GST or other indirect tax treatment shall be determined based on the legal nature of the Property and transaction and shall be borne by the Party legally responsible for it.
 9.4 Each Party shall provide documents reasonably required for tax compliance, withholding and statutory reporting.
 10. REPRESENTATIONS AND WARRANTIES OF THE SELLER
 The Seller represents and warrants that: (a) it is duly incorporated and authorised to execute this Agreement; (b) execution does not violate its constitutional documents or material contractual obligations; (c) it has authority to transfer the Property; (d) there are no undisclosed Encumbrances; (e) no undisclosed agreement to sell, lease, licence or transfer exists; (f) no material litigation or governmental proceeding affecting title or possession has been concealed; (g) information supplied concerning the Property is materially accurate; and (h) all material property dues payable by the Seller up to Completion will be settled.
 11. REPRESENTATIONS OF THE PURCHASER
 The Purchaser represents that it has corporate authority to enter into this Agreement and, subject to its terms, has or will have sufficient funds to meet its payment obligations.
 12. INDEMNITY
 12.1 The Seller shall indemnify the Purchaser against losses arising from breach of Seller warranties, defective title, undisclosed Encumbrances, pre-Completion liabilities, fraud or wilful misconduct.
 12.2 The Purchaser shall indemnify the Seller against losses arising from the Purchaser's material breach, fraud or wilful misconduct.
 12.3 Claims relating to title, fraud or intentional misconduct shall survive Completion notwithstanding any general contractual claim period.
 13. DEFAULT AND TERMINATION
 13.1 If the Purchaser fails to make a payment when due and does not cure the default within 10 Business Days after written notice, the Seller may exercise contractual remedies subject to applicable law.
 13.2 If the Seller materially breaches its title, transfer or completion obligations and fails to cure the breach within 10 Business Days after written notice, the Purchaser may terminate this Agreement and seek refund of amounts paid, together with applicable contractual/legal remedies.
 13.3 The Purchaser may terminate immediately for material fraud, inability to transfer title, or discovery of a material undisclosed Encumbrance that cannot reasonably be cured before Completion.
 13.4 Termination shall not affect accrued rights or provisions intended to survive termination.
 14. CONFIDENTIALITY
 Each Party shall keep confidential all non-public information received in connection with the transaction, except disclosures required by law, regulators, courts, professional advisers or financing parties subject to appropriate confidentiality obligations.
 15. FORCE MAJEURE
 Neither Party shall be liable for delay caused by events beyond its reasonable control, provided the affected Party promptly notifies the other and takes reasonable steps to mitigate the delay. This clause does not excuse payment obligations already due.
 16. NOTICES
 Notices shall be in writing and delivered by hand, recognised courier or email to the following addresses:
 Seller: Apex Industrial Assets Private Limited, 201, Western Business Centre, Andheri East, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400069; Email: legal@apexindustrialassets.example
 Purchaser: LMN Asset Pvt. Ltd., 501, Business Tower, Andheri East, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400069; Email: legal@lmnaasset.example
 17. ASSIGNMENT
 Neither Party may assign its rights or obligations without prior written consent of the other Party, except that the Purchaser may assign to an affiliate or financing entity in connection with the transaction, subject to applicable law.
 18. DISPUTE RESOLUTION AND GOVERNING LAW
 18.1 This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of India.
 18.2 The Parties shall first attempt to resolve disputes through good-faith discussions between senior authorised representatives.
 18.3 If unresolved within 30 days, the dispute shall be referred to arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, as amended.
 18.4 The tribunal shall consist of one arbitrator mutually appointed by the Parties. The seat and venue shall be Mumbai, Maharashtra, and the language shall be English.
 18.5 Courts at Mumbai shall have jurisdiction for interim relief and other matters permitted by law.
 19. GENERAL
 19.1 This Agreement and its Schedules constitute the entire agreement concerning the sale and purchase of the Property.
 19.2 Amendments must be in writing and signed by both Parties.
 19.3 If any provision is invalid, the remaining provisions shall continue in force.
 19.4 No waiver is effective unless in writing.
 19.5 This Agreement may be executed in counterparts and electronically to the extent legally permissible.
 19.6 Headings are for convenience and do not affect interpretation.

documents.name: Unity-Suggestions.docx
documents.extractedText:
PoC's for Unity Bank
 Collateral management + small lending
 T hough I am looking at from the fraud angle but this can be flipped (where Unity can say RBI has a common ledger), and we can pitch this as the Inveniam + Zanbato proposition (without naming them) . Where I say digital footprint to protect from fraud, they can be also pitched as the digital footprint of an asset for its valuation, change in status/nature so on and so forth. The double-pledging / duplicate collateral fraud (the same warehouse receipt, gold, or invoice pledged to multiple lenders , is behind India's biggest banking frauds).
 What it looks like: A shared, permissioned ledger where every pledged asset such as gold, warehouse receipts, invoices, property gets a single digital fingerprint the moment it's pledged. Any other bank or NBFC checking that asset instantly sees it's already collateralized. No more paper-based registries with lag time that fraudsters exploit.
 Real precedent, adapted small: blockchain turns collateral management from a static, periodic process into a dynamic one , margin requirements can be monitored continuously, and smart contracts can automatically trigger a margin call or even a liquidation sequence the moment collateral value drops below a threshold, instead of a credit officer manually checking valuations weekly.
 On the lending side: smart-contract-based automation of loan agreements typically brings a 15-60% reduction in operational cost , real money for a small bank's back office. Bank of China Hong Kong is a good proof point: it cut property valuation time for mortgage deals from days to seconds using blockchain-verified data, and now 85% of its mortgage-related valuations run through that system.
 India-specific hook: SBI already ran a live example combining CBDC + trade collateral . A State Bank of India consortium completed a $50 million trade finance transaction with a UAE bank using programmable e₹-W tokens that automatically released payment upon shipping document verification. Unity Bank doesn't need SBI's scale to copy the idea , automatic, condition-based release of funds against verified collateral , for something as simple as gold loans or agri -warehouse receipt financing (which ties nicely into India's WDRA e-NWR system, already digital, and a natural blockchain candidate).
 Why this combo is a strong pitch internally: it's not "blockchain for blockchain's sake" , it directly reduces fraud risk (a board-level concern), cuts loan processing cost and doesn't require RBI sign-of f , so Unity Bank could pilot it faster and on its own timeline.
 Blockchain-based trade finance (digitizing letters of credit & bills of lading) (I am very hopeful about our existing TF solution to be expanded/repurposed to do this).
 If Unity Bank serves any SME exporters/importers (textiles, agri -commodities, pharma, gems & jewellery in India), this is a direct pain-point solver.
 What it looks like: Replace paper LCs and bills of lading , which today involve manual verification, couriers, and multi-day reconciliation , with a shared digital ledger that all parties (bank, exporter, importer, shipping line) can trust instantly.
 Why it's exciting for them: operational cost reduction in banking trade operations reaches thirty to forty-five percent through automation of reconciliation, compliance checks, and multi-party coordination processes. That's a real, measurable cost story to take to the board. It also cuts fraud ; permissioned networks let a bank financing a trade see shipment status while sensitive pricing and customer data stay confidential to the relevant parties, which matters a lot for SME clients worried about competitors seeing their deals.
 Momentum: as of early 2026, legislation recognizing electronic trade records as legally equivalent to paper documents had been adopted in 13 jurisdictions , the legal groundwork is being laid globally, so a small bank moving now would be ahead of the curve rather than betting on unproven tech
 Where they say Adverse (apologies if I forgot the name) can give them the data points, as I was explaining, what we bring is like the OS of iPhone. While on the surface everyone can give the features, we give both the features and the protection of the data layer.

 SALE AGREEMENT
 This Sale Agreement (the "Agreement") is made and executed on 30 September 2026 (the "Agreement Date") by and between the following parties:
 1. Apex Industrial Assets Private Limited, a company incorporated under the laws of India, having its registered office at 201, Western Business Centre, Andheri East, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400069, hereinafter referred to as the "Seller"; and
 2. LMN Asset Pvt. Ltd., a company incorporated under the laws of India, having its registered office at 501, Business Tower, Andheri East, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400069, hereinafter referred to as the "Purchaser".
 The Seller and the Purchaser are individually referred to as a "Party" and collectively as the "Parties".
 RECITALS
 A. The Seller represents that it is the lawful owner of the commercial office premises described in Schedule 1 (the "Property") and has the right and authority to sell and transfer the Property.
 B. The Purchaser has agreed to purchase the Property from the Seller for the consideration and on the terms set out in this Agreement.
 C. The Parties wish to record the terms governing the sale, purchase, transfer of title, payment, possession, registration and completion of the transaction.
 1. DEFINITIONS
 Term
 Meaning
 Agreement
 This Sale Agreement together with its Schedules and any written amendments.
 Completion

 Property

 Completion Documents
 The title, transfer, possession, tax, statutory and other documents specified in Schedule 3.
 2. AGREEMENT TO SELL AND PURCHASE
 2.1 The Seller agrees to sell, convey, assign and transfer the Property to the Purchaser, and the Purchaser agrees to purchase and accept the Property, free from all undisclosed Encumbrances and third-party claims.
 2.2 The sale includes the Property and all rights, easements, access rights, common-area rights and appurtenant rights legally attached to it, together with the fixtures and improvements expressly included in Schedule 1.
 2.3 The Seller shall not sell, agree to sell, mortgage, lease, license, encumber or otherwise dispose of the Property between the Agreement Date and Completion.
 3. PURCHASE PRICE
 3.1 The total Purchase Price for the Property is ₹12,50,00,000 (Rupees Twelve Crore Fifty Lakh Only).
 3.2 The Parties acknowledge that the Purchase Price is consistent with the indicative valuation conclusion of ₹12.50 crore contained in the related valuation memorandum dated 30 September 2026.
 3.3 The Purchase Price is subject to applicable taxes, duties and statutory charges as allocated under Clause 9 and Schedule 2.
 4. PAYMENT TERMS
 4.1 The Purchaser shall pay the Purchase Price as follows:
 a) ₹1,25,00,000 as earnest money/deposit, payable on execution of this Agreement;
 b) ₹3,75,00,000 as the second instalment upon satisfaction of the conditions precedent and completion of agreed title due diligence; and
 c) ₹7,50,00,000 as the balance consideration at Completion against delivery of the Completion Documents, possession and execution/registration of the applicable transfer instrument.
 4.2 Payments shall be made through normal banking channels to the Seller's designated account, subject to applicable law.
 4.3 The Seller shall issue appropriate receipts and tax invoices/documents where legally required.
 5. CONDITIONS PRECEDENT
 Completion is conditional upon: (a) satisfactory verification of the Seller's title; (b) confirmation that the Property is free of undisclosed Encumbrances; (c) verification of applicable approvals and permitted commercial use; (d) receipt of required corporate, regulatory or third-party approvals; (e) no material adverse litigation or governmental action affecting the Property; and (f) execution of all required ancillary documents.
 6. TITLE AND SELLER'S COVENANTS
 6.1 The Seller represents and warrants that it has good, valid and transferable title to the Property and full authority to enter into and complete the sale.
 6.2 The Seller shall provide the Purchaser with copies/originals, as applicable, of title deeds, prior conveyances, sanctioned plans, completion/occupancy documentation, tax records, society/association records and other relevant property documents.
 6.3 The Seller shall discharge all monetary liabilities, taxes, maintenance dues, utility dues and other obligations attributable to the period up to Completion, unless expressly allocated otherwise in Schedule 2.
 6.4 The Seller shall procure release/discharge of any disclosed mortgage or other Encumbrance before or simultaneously with Completion.
 7. INSPECTION AND PROPERTY CONDITION
 7.1 The Purchaser shall have reasonable access to inspect the Property and its documents before Completion.
 7.2 The Property shall be delivered in substantially the condition represented by the Seller, subject to ordinary wear and tear.
 7.3 Inspection or acceptance shall not waive the Purchaser's rights in respect of fraud, defective title, concealed defects or breach of the Seller's express representations and warranties.
 8. COMPLETION, POSSESSION AND TRANSFER
 8.1 Completion shall occur on 30 September 2026 at [registered office/sub-registrar office/other agreed location], subject to satisfaction of the conditions precedent.
 8.2 At Completion, the Seller shall deliver vacant and peaceful possession of the Property to the Purchaser, unless Schedule 1 expressly states otherwise.
 8.3 The Parties shall execute and register the applicable sale deed/conveyance or other instrument required to transfer legal title.
 8.4 Risk in the Property shall pass to the Purchaser upon Completion and delivery of possession, except to the extent caused by the Seller's breach or wilful misconduct.
 8.5 The Seller shall cooperate with mutation, registration, society/association transfer and other post-completion formalities.
 9. TAXES, STAMP DUTY AND REGISTRATION
 9.1 Stamp duty and registration charges relating to the instrument of transfer shall be borne by the Purchaser unless mandatory law requires otherwise.
 9.2 Taxes attributable to the Seller's ownership or period before Completion shall be borne by the Seller.
 9.3 Any applicable GST or other indirect tax treatment shall be determined based on the legal nature of the Property and transaction and shall be borne by the Party legally responsible for it.
 9.4 Each Party shall provide documents reasonably required for tax compliance, withholding and statutory reporting.
 10. REPRESENTATIONS AND WARRANTIES OF THE SELLER
 The Seller represents and warrants that: (a) it is duly incorporated and authorised to execute this Agreement; (b) execution does not violate its constitutional documents or material contractual obligations; (c) it has authority to transfer the Property; (d) there are no undisclosed Encumbrances; (e) no undisclosed agreement to sell, lease, licence or transfer exists; (f) no material litigation or governmental proceeding affecting title or possession has been concealed; (g) information supplied concerning the Property is materially accurate; and (h) all material property dues payable by the Seller up to Completion will be settled.
 11. REPRESENTATIONS OF THE PURCHASER
 The Purchaser represents that it has corporate authority to enter into this Agreement and, subject to its terms, has or will have sufficient funds to meet its payment obligations.
 12. INDEMNITY
 12.1 The Seller shall indemnify the Purchaser against losses arising from breach of Seller warranties, defective title, undisclosed Encumbrances, pre-Completion liabilities, fraud or wilful misconduct.
 12.2 The Purchaser shall indemnify the Seller against losses arising from the Purchaser's material breach, fraud or wilful misconduct.
 12.3 Claims relating to title, fraud or intentional misconduct shall survive Completion notwithstanding any general contractual claim period.
 13. DEFAULT AND TERMINATION
 13.1 If the Purchaser fails to make a payment when due and does not cure the default within 10 Business Days after written notice, the Seller may exercise contractual remedies subject to applicable law.
 13.2 If the Seller materially breaches its title, transfer or completion obligations and fails to cure the breach within 10 Business Days after written notice, the Purchaser may terminate this Agreement and seek refund of amounts paid, together with applicable contractual/legal remedies.
 13.3 The Purchaser may terminate immediately for material fraud, inability to transfer title, or discovery of a material undisclosed Encumbrance that cannot reasonably be cured before Completion.
 13.4 Termination shall not affect accrued rights or provisions intended to survive termination.
 14. CONFIDENTIALITY
 Each Party shall keep confidential all non-public information received in connection with the transaction, except disclosures required by law, regulators, courts, professional advisers or financing parties subject to appropriate confidentiality obligations.
 15. FORCE MAJEURE
 Neither Party shall be liable for delay caused by events beyond its reasonable control, provided the affected Party promptly notifies the other and takes reasonable steps to mitigate the delay. This clause does not excuse payment obligations already due.
 16. NOTICES
 Notices shall be in writing and delivered by hand, recognised courier or email to the following addresses:
 Seller: Apex Industrial Assets Private Limited, 201, Western Business Centre, Andheri East, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400069; Email: legal@apexindustrialassets.example
 Purchaser: LMN Asset Pvt. Ltd., 501, Business Tower, Andheri East, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400069; Email: legal@lmnaasset.example
 17. ASSIGNMENT
 Neither Party may assign its rights or obligations without prior written consent of the other Party, except that the Purchaser may assign to an affiliate or financing entity in connection with the transaction, subject to applicable law.
 18. DISPUTE RESOLUTION AND GOVERNING LAW
 18.1 This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of India.
 18.2 The Parties shall first attempt to resolve disputes through good-faith discussions between senior authorised representatives.
 18.3 If unresolved within 30 days, the dispute shall be referred to arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, as amended.
 18.4 The tribunal shall consist of one arbitrator mutually appointed by the Parties. The seat and venue shall be Mumbai, Maharashtra, and the language shall be English.
 18.5 Courts at Mumbai shall have jurisdiction for interim relief and other matters permitted by law.
 19. GENERAL
 19.1 This Agreement and its Schedules constitute the entire agreement concerning the sale and purchase of the Property.
 19.2 Amendments must be in writing and signed by both Parties.
 19.3 If any provision is invalid, the remaining provisions shall continue in force.
 19.4 No waiver is effective unless in writing.
 19.5 This Agreement may be executed in counterparts and electronically to the extent legally permissible.
 19.6 Headings are for convenience and do not affect interpretation.

Unity Bank doesn't need SBI's scale to copy the idea , automatic, condition-based release of funds against verified collateral , for something as simple as gold loans or agri -warehouse receipt financing (which ties nicely into India's WDRA e-NWR system, already digital, and a natural blockchain candidate).

Harbourview Tower is marked at GBP 92.8m as of 30 June 2026, up from the GBP 86.4m acquisition price. Overall risk is moderate (34).
